title: Misinformation of COVID-19 vaccines and vaccine hesitancy
screen_reason: Study 1 is a US survey (n = 505 MTurk full-time workers, March 2021) with an open-ended item asking what COVID-19 vaccine misinformation respondents had heard; 57.6% of the 488 coded respondents reported being exposed to one or more pieces of vaccine misinformation (207, 42.4%, reported hearing none). That is a share of survey respondents reporting exposure, i.e. RECALL with a denominator. Study 2 measures BELIEF in false vaccine statements only, which the protocol excludes, so it contributes no rows.

estimates.platform: not platform-specific (open-ended question about misinformation 'heard', no channel specified)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who reported having heard one or more pieces of misinformation or false claims about COVID-19 vaccines
estimates.value_raw: 57.6% of participants reported being exposed to one or more pieces of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation; complementarily, Table 1 records 207 respondents (42.4%) as 'I didn't hear any misinformation related to COVID vaccines' out of the 488 coded responses (281 = 488 - 207 gives 57.58%)
estimates.denominator: 488 US full-time working adults recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk who answered the open-ended vaccine-misinformation item (of 505 participants; 17 did not answer). Sample: 46.3% women, 70.4% White, 78.5% bachelor's degree or higher, mean age 37.54 (SD 10.30), all working at least 40 h/week
estimates.definition: Respondent's free-text answer to 'Have you heard about any misinformation or false claims related to the COVID-19 vaccines?' was coded to anything other than 'I didn't hear any misinformation related to COVID vaccines' - 14 misinformation types (microchip, dangerous/harmful, cause death, DNA alteration, cause COVID-19, government control, sterilization, other diseases, ineffective, autism, fetal cells, mark of the beast, zombies) plus an 'Others (not relevant)' bucket and a 'Facts perceived as misinformation' bucket
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation, also called as fake news, refers to any inaccurate claims or depictions and disinformation is a subset of misinformation 'intended to mislead'13 (para. 3)."
estimates.source_quote: Content analysis of the open-ended responses in Study 1 revealed that 57.6% of the participants reported being exposed to one or more pieces of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Discussion, p. 5; Results for study 1, p. 3; Table 1, p. 3; Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported exposure to a single open-ended item; no verification that what respondents reported was in fact misinformation, and no measure of whether they believed it. Three researchers with PhDs in Communication or Psychology built a common coding scheme on the same 40 responses, checked consistency on 50 further responses and resolved differences by discussion, then DIVIDED the 488 responses and each coded 163 independently - so the analysed responses were single-coded and no kappa or other reliability statistic is reported. The authors flag that non-reporters may have been exposed without recognising the content as inaccurate.
estimates.moderator_quote: "Participants were asked to answer the following open-ended questionnaire: 'Have you heard about any misinformation or false claims related to the COVID-19 vaccines? If so, please write down any false information you have come across.'"
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALLS an adjudicator should see. (a) The paper carries THREE mutually inconsistent denominators for the same quantity: the Results text says 'Out of 426 participants, 207 participants (42.42%) indicated that they did not hear any misinformation' - but 207/426 = 48.6%, whereas 207/488 = 42.42%, and Table 1's percentages (62 = 12.7%, 52 = 10.6%) all divide by 488. The Discussion separately says 'about 41%' reported hearing none, which is 207/505. I therefore treat 488 (all coded responses) as the operative denominator, which is also what reproduces the headline 57.6% (281/488 = 57.58%). (b) The 281-respondent numerator INCLUDES the 62 respondents whose answers were coded 'Others (not relevant)' (e.g. 'many', 'false') and the 15 coded 'Facts related to COVID-19 vaccines were perceived as misinformation'. A stricter reading that removes those from the numerator would give (281 - 62 - 15)/488 = 42.2%, but that is a cross-category subtraction barred by R8, so the paper's own 57.6% stands with this caveat noted. (c) The measure is unprompted free recall with no channel, window or platform specified, which makes it not comparable to closed-item exposure measures. (d) population_scope coded general_public: the sample is restricted to adults working 40+ h/week ('full-time working professionals') but is not a specific occupational profession.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Table 1 gives the share of respondents reporting each individual misinformation type (microchip 10.6%, dangerous/harmful 7.4%, cause death 7.2%, DNA alteration 5.3%, cause COVID-19 4.7%, government control 4.1%, sterilization 3.5%, other diseases 3.5%, ineffective 3.1%, facts perceived as misinformation 3.1%, autism 2.7%, fetal cells 1.4%, mark of the beast 0.8%, zombies 0.4%). I did not make rows for these: they are sub-types of the single headline exposure estimate, respondents could give more than one answer (70 of the 281 did) so the percentages overlap and sum past 100, and none is the paper's headline. 2) ALL of Study 2 is excluded by the protocol: the 10-item true/false knowledge test (Table 5) measures BELIEF in false claims, e.g. 31.3% answered 'true' to 'COVID-19 vaccines can give you COVID-19', 27.7% to 'It can be safer to get a disease than to get its vaccine', 25.6% to 'COVID-19 vaccines can cause infertility', 15.2% to 'COVID-19 mRNA vaccines can alter human DNA', 6.3% to 'COVID-19 vaccines can cause autism'. Belief/susceptibility measures are explicitly outside the review's inclusion rule, so no rows despite being clean shares with a denominator (n = 441 college students, Feb-May 2021). 3) The reported vaccination-coverage figures (US 65.4% fully vaccinated as of 24 March 2022, Germany/Italy/Portugal >75%, Japan 79%, South Korea 86%, Canada 84%) and the CDC 0.002% vaccine-linked death figure are cited from elsewhere, so R8 bars them regardless. 4) Study 2's knowledge score (M = 8.35/10) and hesitancy/intention scales are means, not shares.

rob.design: Study 1 (the only study contributing an estimate): cross-sectional online survey, Amazon Mechanical Turk convenience sample, March 2021, IRB-approved (University of Oklahoma); n = 505 US adults working at least 40 h/week (46.3% women, 70.4% White, 78.5% bachelor's or higher, mean age 37.54, SD 10.30); no response rate or completion time reported. A single open-ended item elicited misinformation heard about COVID-19 vaccines; 17 participants did not answer, leaving 488 coded, of which 62 gave irrelevant answers. Three PhD-level coders developed a scheme on a common set of 40 responses, verified understanding on 50 more, and then split the 488 responses coding 163 each INDEPENDENTLY - i.e. the analysed data are single-coded, with no inter-rater reliability statistic reported. Authors' own limitations: cross-sectional, cannot verify non-exposure claims, samples over 70% White and college-educated and therefore not generalisable to the US population, and the true scale of misinformation exposure could be larger than reported. Study 2: SONA departmental research pool of college students at one university, Feb-May 2021, 597 responses, 156 dropped for incompleteness, n = 441, restricted to unvaccinated 18+; 10-item true/false knowledge test, Vaccine Hesitancy Scale (alpha 0.94), SEM in AMOS with 2000 bootstrap replications.
rob.item6_quote: Have you heard about any misinformation or false claims related to the COVID-19 vaccines? If so, please write down any false information you have come across.
rob.item10_quote: Out of 488 participants, 62 participants provided irrelevant responses (e.g., "many", "false", "learn about the benefits of COVID-19 vaccination based on what experts currently know"). Out of 426 participants, 207 participants (42.42%) indicated that they did not hear any misinformation related to COVID-19 vaccines.
